lead: Temperature is the property that two bodies share when no heat flows between them. The zeroth law makes this usable: if a thermometer agrees with body A and also with body B, then A and B agree with each other, so we can compare them without touching them. That rule underlies every fever thermometer, every server-room cooling alarm and every air-conditioning check in an Indian train coach. This chapter states the law, defines temperature, and shows how a thermometer turns a changing property into a number on the Celsius or Kelvin scale.
prereq: You need: equilibrium ideas from 1.4 Thermodynamic equilibrium and quasi-static process.

sections.h3: The zeroth law and thermal equilibrium

blocks.text: Two bodies are in thermal equilibrium when, after contact through a diathermal wall, no observable change occurs in either body. A diathermal wall lets heat pass; an adiabatic wall does not. The zeroth law states: if body A is in thermal equilibrium with body C, and body B is in thermal equilibrium with body C, then A and B are in thermal equilibrium with each other. C is usually a thermometer.

Use the law as a comparison rule. A thermometer placed in A reaches the same reading as in B only when A and B share the same temperature. Temperature is the property that is equal in thermal equilibrium. Heat flows only when temperatures differ; the direction is from higher temperature to lower temperature. Equal readings mean no net heat flow, not that the bodies hold equal internal energy.

A thermometer needs a thermometric property: a measurable property that changes with thermal state. Common examples are the length of a mercury column, the pressure of a gas held at fixed volume, the electrical resistance of a platinum wire, and the emf of a thermocouple.
The principle of thermometry chooses a property X and defines an empirical temperature θ by a linear relation.

blocks.where: θ is empirical temperature; X is the thermometric property; a and b are constants fixed by two fixed points.

blocks.text: The Celsius scale fixes two points at 1 atm: the ice point at 0 °C (ice and water in equilibrium) and the steam point at 100 °C (water boiling). The interval is divided into 100 equal parts. The Kelvin scale uses the same size degree and shifts the zero: 0 °C = 273.15 K and 100 °C = 373.15 K.

blocks.where: T(K) is absolute temperature in kelvin; t(°C) is Celsius temperature; 273.15 is the offset in kelvin.

blocks.text: A constant-volume gas thermometer measures the pressure of a fixed mass of gas at fixed volume. Its readings depend slightly on the gas, but as pressure tends to zero all gases agree. That limit gives the ideal gas temperature scale. The thermodynamic temperature scale is developed in Unit 3, Thermodynamic temperature scale. Some syllabi call this topic 'concept of temperature and principles of thermometry'.

sections.h3: Using the zeroth law in practice

items: Place the thermometer in body A. Wait until the reading is steady; the thermometer is then in thermal equilibrium with A. Record θ_A.
Place the same thermometer in body B. Wait for a steady reading and record θ_B.
If θ_A = θ_B, the zeroth law says A and B are in thermal equilibrium. If the readings differ, connecting A and B causes net heat flow from the higher reading to the lower reading.

blocks.text: The waiting time matters. A thermometer shows its own temperature, not the body's, until equilibrium is reached. A clinical thermometer held under the tongue for too short a time reads low. A sensor strapped to a server rack gives the rack temperature only after its probe settles. Calibration fixes the scale; the zeroth law fixes the comparison.

figure.caption: Body A and body B each give the same thermometer reading, so the dashed link shows that A and B are in thermal equilibrium. The thermometer C is the referee.

spec.aria: A graph shows body A and body B each in thermal equilibrium with a thermometer C, so the dashed edge marks that A and B are also in thermal equilibrium.

examples.question: A thermometer reads 25.0 °C in body A and 25.0 °C in body B. Body A and body B are then placed in contact. Using the zeroth law, find the direction of heat flow and convert 25.0 °C to kelvin.
steps: The two readings are equal: 25.0 °C in A and 25.0 °C in B.
By the zeroth law, A and B are in thermal equilibrium with each other.
In thermal equilibrium there is no net heat flow when A and B are placed in contact. The direction is therefore 'no net flow'; the temperatures are equal.
examples.answer: No net heat flows between A and B; the temperature is 298.15 K.

traps: Temperature is not heat. Equal thermometer readings mean no net heat flow; body A and body B can have different masses and different internal energies.
The Kelvin offset is 273.15, not 273. Use 273.15 for precise conversion; rounding early shifts the answer.
The ice point is equilibrium ice and water at 1 atm, not any mixture of ice and salt. The steam point is water boiling at 1 atm, not steam at any pressure.
A thermometer reads correctly only after it reaches thermal equilibrium with the body. A reading taken while the thermometer is still warming is not the body temperature.
The zeroth law gives equality of temperature. It does not by itself give an absolute zero or a heat quantity.

quiz.q: State the zeroth law of thermodynamics.
quiz.a: If A is in thermal equilibrium with C and B is in thermal equilibrium with C, then A and B are in thermal equilibrium with each other.

quiz.q: Why must a thermometer be in thermal equilibrium with a body before its reading is used?
quiz.a: The thermometer shows its own temperature. Only at equilibrium is its temperature equal to the body's, so the reading represents the body.

quiz.q: A thermometer reads 30 °C in body A and 32 °C in body B. When A and B are connected, which way does net heat flow?
quiz.a: From B to A, because B is at higher temperature. Net heat flow stops when both reach the same temperature.

quiz.q: Bodies A and B have the same thermometer reading but different masses and materials. What can you conclude about their temperature, internal energy, and heat content?
quiz.a: Their temperatures are equal. Their internal energies need not be equal, and heat is not a property stored in a body; heat is energy in transit.
Length of a mercury column; pressure of a gas at fixed volume. Also acceptable: resistance of a platinum wire; emf of a thermocouple.

quiz.q: What is the difference between empirical temperature and thermodynamic temperature?
quiz.a: Empirical temperature is read from a chosen thermometric property and scale. Thermodynamic temperature is defined by the second law and is independent of the working substance; the ideal gas scale approaches it.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern calibration uses platinum resistance thermometers and thermocouples traceable to the International Temperature Scale of 1990 (ITS-90), with fixed points such as the triple point of water. The kelvin was redefined in 2019 using the Boltzmann constant, so its realization now rests on a fundamental constant. Data-centre cooling and vaccine cold chains depend on calibrated sensors and uncertainty budgets. Search next: ITS-90 fixed points, constant-volume gas thermometer, Boltzmann constant redefinition.
